newsitem.title: USA: Everglades group sues U.S. Sugar for $900 million.
newsitem.headline: Everglades group sues U.S. Sugar for $900 million.

text.p: An environmental group filed a $900-million lawsuit Friday against U.S. Sugar Corp, alleging the company deceived Florida voters during a referendum campaign last fall on a proposed sugar tax, the group said.

The lawsuit, filed by Save Our Everglades in circuit court in the state capital, alleged that U.S. Sugar, through a campaign organisation called Citizens to Save Jobs and Stop Unfair Taxes, sent mailings intended to "illegally influence, deceive and trick" voters, the group said.

The Amendment 4 tax proposal, a constitutional revision that would have collected an estimated $900 million from sugar producers over 25 years for restoration of the fragile Florida wetland, was defeated in a statewide referendum Nov. 6.

During the fiercely contested campaign -- the most expensive in state history -- sugar companies spent an estimated $24 million to persuade voters to defeat the penny-a-pound tax, claiming it would cost Florida thousands of jobs and put the industry out of business.
"The campaign waged against Amendment 4 was false from start to finish," Thom Rumberger, general counsel for the group, said in a statement.
U.S. Sugar vice president Robert Buker said the lawsuit would be defeated because political debate was protected by the First Amendment.
"They'll lose this case. There's no merit to it whatsoever," he said.

Officials of the group said the lawsuit alleged that privately held U.S. Sugar, one of the nation's largest sugar farming companies, violated the state's statute on influencing voting. Several mailings falsely declared that the constitutional amendment for the sugar fee would increase residents' property taxes, the lawsuit said.

The amendment said the tax would be levied against sugar companies and made no mention of property tax increases. The group said polling data showed nine percent of those voting "no" said they thought the amendment would increase property taxes.
"As a result of these false mailings, U.S. Sugar intentionally shifted $900 million of the cost of Everglades restoration from U.S. Sugar and other polluters to innocent taxpayers," Rumberger said.

Buker said the lawsuit was really a countersuit to one filed by U.S. Sugar three months ago, in which the company claimed SOS received public campaign financing by claiming it had no money when in fact it had $11 million in its war chest.

Environmentalists and scientists have long contended that sugar plantation fertilisers have polluted the Everglades water and damaged the slow-moving "river of grass" by increasing growth of plants that crowd out native vegetation.
